$comment: Facts v2 for the home-page Fact Shuffler. Niches: obscure geography/geopolitics, weird science & space, art-history deep cuts, etymology oddities. One is shown at random on load; 'next fact' cycles randomly without repeating until all are seen (tracked in sessionStorage), then resets.

items.headline: The land nobody wants
items.body: Bir Tawil, a desert patch between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither country — claiming it would mean surrendering a larger, more valuable territory next door. It's one of the only unclaimed lands on Earth.

items.headline: A town sliced by 30 borders
items.body: Baarle, on the Belgium–Netherlands border, contains 30 enclaves — some houses straddle the line, so the front door's position decides which country taxes you.

items.headline: Tomorrow is 3.8 km away
items.body: The two Diomede Islands in the Bering Strait sit 3.8 km apart but 21 hours apart in time — from Little Diomede (USA) you can look across at tomorrow in Russia.

items.headline: You are being shot through right now
items.body: About 100 trillion neutrinos pass through your body every second — through you, the Earth, and out the other side — almost never touching a single atom.

items.headline: The Sun is deafeningly loud
items.body: If space carried sound, the Sun's surface convection would roar at roughly 100 dB by the time it reached Earth — a permanent rock concert, 150 million km away.

items.headline: We still bounce lasers off the Moon
items.body: Apollo astronauts left retroreflector mirrors on the lunar surface in 1969. Observatories still fire lasers at them to measure the Moon's distance — it drifts 3.8 cm farther every year.

items.headline: Blue cost more than gold
items.body: Renaissance ultramarine was ground from lapis lazuli mined only in Afghanistan. It was so expensive that contracts specified exactly how much could be used — which is why Mary's robe is always blue.

items.headline: Vermeer may have traced light itself
items.body: Optical evidence suggests Vermeer used a camera obscura — a darkened room projecting the scene onto his canvas. His out-of-focus highlights match lens artifacts no naked eye would see.

items.headline: The Great Wave is chemically European
items.body: Hokusai's iconic blue is Prussian blue — a pigment invented by accident in a Berlin lab and shipped to Japan, where it made the most Japanese image ever printed.

items.headline: Your salary is salt
items.body: 'Salary' comes from the Latin salarium — money given to Roman soldiers, tied by ancient authors to salt purchases. Being 'worth your salt' is the same transaction, 2,000 years later.

items.headline: Quarantine means exactly forty
items.body: Plague-era Venice made arriving ships wait quaranta giorni — forty days — before docking. The number wore off; the word never did.

items.headline: Deadlines used to kill you
items.body: In Civil War prison camps, the 'dead line' was a boundary; prisoners who crossed it were shot. Editors adopted the word — the stakes have only slightly improved.

items.headline: An island that sings in chords
items.body: Sardinian cantu a tenore is sung by four men producing overtones so unusual that UNESCO protects it — one voice imitates a sheep, another the wind.

items.headline: The landlocked country with a navy
items.body: Mongolia — double-landlocked from any ocean by Russia and China — has kept a tiny navy on Lake Khövsgöl. For years it consisted of one tugboat and seven sailors.

items.headline: The dark night sky is evidence
items.body: If the universe were infinite and eternal, every line of sight would end on a star and the night sky would blaze white. Darkness at night is proof the universe had a beginning.
